guideTitle: The Best Under-Desk Ellipticals for Moving During the Workday
metaTitle: Best Under-Desk Ellipticals for Home Offices (2026)
metaDescription: We compared under-desk ellipticals on user weight rating, resistance, noise-relevant design, portability and tracking, from compact pedal units to a motorized model.
introParagraphs: An under-desk elliptical has to fit two things at once: the space between the floor and the underside of your desk, and the rhythm of a working day, which usually means staying quiet enough for calls. Measure your usable clearance, including any crossbars or drawers, before looking at resistance levels or apps.

The eight models below differ more than their similar shapes suggest. Maximum user weight ranges from 150 to 300 lb, resistance from 8 to 12 levels, and one model is motorized, moving your legs for you rather than asking you to pedal.
Our comparison is based on published specifications, listed features and price position, not hands-on testing.

cubii-jr1-elliptical.badge: Best Compact Pick with App Tracking
cubii-jr1-elliptical.summary: A compact, battery-powered unit with 8 magnetic resistance levels and Bluetooth tracking, rated to 150 lb.
cubii-jr1-elliptical.description:
The Cubii JR1 suits a small desk setup where tracking matters: it is compact, runs on batteries so there's no cord to route, and syncs strides, distance and calories to the Cubii app over Bluetooth.

It has 8 levels of manual magnetic resistance, an 18-inch stride and an LCD display, and weighs 25.4 lb.

Its limit is capacity: at 150 lb, it has the lowest maximum user weight here, well below the 250 to 300 lb ratings of most alternatives. Check that figure before anything else.
cons: Lowest user weight rating here, 150 lb
Fewer resistance levels than the Cubii GO or Total Body V2
Costs more than similar non-app models
cubii-jr1-elliptical.bestFor: Lighter users who want app-based tracking in a compact, cord-free unit.
cubii-jr1-elliptical.skipIf: You need a higher weight rating; the Sunny SF-E3872 is rated to 250 lb for less.

sunny-health-sf-e3872-elliptical.summary: A belt-drive magnetic unit that ships fully assembled, rated to 250 lb.
sunny-health-sf-e3872-elliptical.description:
The Sunny SF-E3872 is the simplest to get going: it ships fully assembled, with 8 levels of belt-drive magnetic resistance and a monitor showing time, speed, calories and distance.

Sunny describes a pedal path shaped to keep knees clear of the desk. It weighs 25 lb and is rated for users up to 250 lb, a higher ceiling than the more expensive Cubii JR1.

There's no Bluetooth or app, and at the time of writing it was not quite the cheapest model here; the Stamina E1000 and LifePro FlexStride Plus were listed slightly lower.
cons: No app or Bluetooth
Basic monitor
Not the lowest price here at the time of writing
sunny-health-sf-e3872-elliptical.bestFor: Anyone who wants a quiet-by-design unit they can use out of the box.
sunny-health-sf-e3872-elliptical.skipIf: You want your sessions logged in an app; the LifePro FlexStride Plus adds Bluetooth at a similar price.

stamina-inmotion-e1000-elliptical.badge: Best for Standing or Seated Use
stamina-inmotion-e1000-elliptical.summary: The lowest-priced model here, and the only one designed for both standing and seated use.
stamina-inmotion-e1000-elliptical.description:
The Stamina InMotion E1000 stands apart because it works in two positions: seated under a desk, or standing, for example at a counter. It was also the lowest-priced model here at the time of writing.

It has 8 levels of magnetic resistance, forward and reverse pedaling, an electronic monitor and müüv app support, and is rated for users up to 250 lb at 24 lb in weight.

The dual-mode design adds some bulk compared with a pure under-desk unit, and its tracking is more basic than the Cubii models' Bluetooth app.
pros: Lowest price here at the time of writing
cons: Bulkier than a dedicated under-desk unit
More basic tracking than the Cubii models
Standing use needs its own floor space
stamina-inmotion-e1000-elliptical.bestFor: Anyone who wants to use the same machine seated at a desk and standing.
stamina-inmotion-e1000-elliptical.skipIf: You only use it seated under a low desk; a compact unit like the Sunny SF-E3872 is more focused.

deskcycle-ellipse-elliptical.summary: A steel-frame unit with extra-large adjustable pedals and a separate display stand.
deskcycle-ellipse-elliptical.description:
The DeskCycle Ellipse is the better fit for larger shoe sizes: its extra-large, adjustable pedals are the largest here, on a steel frame with 8 levels of magnetic resistance that DeskCycle describes as ranging from very easy to hard.

Its 6-function LCD sits on a separate stand, so the display stays visible without being in the way of your feet. DeskCycle describes operation as whisper-quiet.

At 30 lb it is the heaviest model here, which makes it less convenient to move, and the display stand takes a little extra space.
cons: Heaviest model here at 30 lb
Display stand adds footprint
User weight rating not stated in the listing summary
deskcycle-ellipse-elliptical.bestFor: Larger feet, or anyone who wants the display off the floor and in view.
deskcycle-ellipse-elliptical.skipIf: You move the unit often; the Cubii GO has wheels and a handle.

lifepro-flexstride-plus-elliptical.summary: 300 lb rating, Bluetooth tracking, a two-year warranty and a mat, tether, band and stoppers included.
lifepro-flexstride-plus-elliptical.description:
The LifePro FlexStride Plus offers the most for its price on paper: a 300 lb maximum user weight, Bluetooth app tracking and a two-year warranty, at under $120 at the time of writing.

Its LCD shows time, distance, strides, RPM and calories, and the box includes a floor mat, a tether strap, a yoga band and wheel stoppers. It weighs 28.7 lb.

It has 8 resistance levels, fewer than the Cubii GO or Total Body V2, and you may not need every accessory.
specs: Display: time, distance, strides, RPM, calories
pros: 300 lb rating at a low price
Mat, tether, band and stoppers included
cons: 8 resistance levels
Extra accessories you may not use
Heavier than the Cubii JR1 or Sunny
lifepro-flexstride-plus-elliptical.bestFor: Heavier users who want app tracking without paying Cubii prices.
lifepro-flexstride-plus-elliptical.skipIf: You want more resistance levels; the Cubii Total Body V2 offers 12.

cubii-go-elliptical.summary: 10 resistance levels, a 300 lb rating, and built-in wheels with a telescoping handle.
cubii-go-elliptical.description:
The Cubii GO is designed to move: built-in wheels and a double telescoping handle let you roll it between rooms, and its aluminum frame keeps it manageable.

It has 10 levels of magnetic resistance and uses what Cubii calls a ZeroGravitii flywheel, designed for quiet operation. It is rated for 300 lb and syncs to the Cubii app.

It was the most expensive model here at the time of writing, and it has less buyer feedback than the JR1. If it will stay under one desk, the LifePro offers the same weight rating for about half the price.
pros: Wheels and handle for moving it
cons: Most expensive here at the time of writing
Less buyer feedback than the JR1
Portability matters little if it stays put
cubii-go-elliptical.bestFor: Anyone who moves between a desk, a sofa and other rooms during the day.
cubii-go-elliptical.skipIf: It will live under one desk; the LifePro FlexStride Plus matches the 300 lb rating for less.

cubii-total-body-v2-elliptical.summary: 12 resistance levels plus a resistance-band pulley system for arms, rated to 300 lb.
cubii-total-body-v2-elliptical.description:
The Cubii Total Body V2 is the only model here that adds upper-body work: a resistance-band pulley system lets you train your arms alongside the pedaling.

It has 12 levels of magnetic resistance, the widest range here, an LCD display and alloy steel construction. Cubii rates it for users up to 300 lb and up to 7 feet tall.

The pulley hardware gives it a larger footprint than pedal-only units, and it costs more than the entry models.
specs: Max user weight: 300 lb; height up to 7 ft (per Cubii)
cons: Larger footprint
Costs more than entry models
Band work is harder to combine with typing
cubii-total-body-v2-elliptical.bestFor: Using breaks for arm and leg work, rather than pedaling while you type.
cubii-total-body-v2-elliptical.skipIf: You only want to pedal while working; a pedal-only unit is smaller and cheaper.

exerpeutic-2000m-elliptical.summary: An electric model that moves your legs for you, controlled by a corded remote.
exerpeutic-2000m-elliptical.description:
The Exerpeutic 2000M is a different kind of product: an electric motor moves the pedals, so the motion is passive rather than something you drive yourself.

A hand-held remote on a 6-foot cord sets speed and an automatic 15-minute timer without bending down. The foldable pedals have adjustable straps and can be used for arms as well as legs, and a floor mat is included. It is rated for users up to 286 lb.

Passive movement is not the same as a pedaling workout, and it needs a power outlet near your desk.
pros: Can be used for arms or legs
cons: Not an active workout
Needs an outlet
Lower weight rating than the 300 lb models
exerpeutic-2000m-elliptical.bestFor: Readers who want passive leg movement rather than exercise.
exerpeutic-2000m-elliptical.skipIf: You want to exercise while working; any of the manual models suits that better.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Measure from the floor to the lowest point under your desk, including crossbars and drawers, and compare it with the unit's height at the top of the pedal stroke as listed.
Ratings here range from 150 lb (Cubii JR1) to 300 lb (LifePro, Cubii GO, Total Body V2). Choose a model rated for you.
Every manual model here uses magnetic resistance, which avoids friction contact. Manufacturer noise claims are not independently measured, so treat them as a guide.
Bluetooth models log sessions in an app; others show them on a display only. If you'll move the unit, wheels and weight matter more than resistance levels.

faq.q: How much clearance do I need under my desk?
faq.a: It depends on the model's height at the top of the pedal stroke. Measure from the floor to the lowest point under your desk, including crossbars and drawers, and compare that with the listed dimensions.

faq.q: Are under-desk ellipticals quiet enough for video calls?
faq.a: The manual models here use magnetic resistance, which avoids friction contact, and several manufacturers describe their units as quiet. Noise also depends on your floor and pedaling speed, so a mat can help.

faq.q: Which has the highest weight rating?
faq.a: The LifePro FlexStride Plus, Cubii GO and Cubii Total Body V2 are rated to 300 lb. The Cubii JR1 is rated to 150 lb.

faq.q: What's the difference between manual and motorized?
faq.a: On a manual model, you drive the pedals. The Exerpeutic 2000M uses a motor to move them, so it provides passive movement rather than exercise.

faq.q: Can I use one with a normal office chair?
faq.a: Yes, the models here are designed for seated use. A chair with casters may roll back as you pedal; a tether strap, like the one included with the LifePro, or a mat can help.

bottomLine: Start with your weight and desk clearance: the Cubii JR1 is compact and cord-free but rated to 150 lb, while the LifePro FlexStride Plus offers a 300 lb rating, app tracking and a two-year warranty for well under the Cubii models' prices at the time of writing.

Choose the Cubii GO if you'll move the unit around, the Total Body V2 for arm work, the Stamina E1000 for standing use, or the DeskCycle Ellipse for larger feet. The Exerpeutic 2000M is for passive movement, not exercise.
